_README: Overload resolution table for `tensor.<method>(...)`, the sibling of
`overloads.json`. Same machine, same rule -- an ordered list of aten
schemas per name, first one that binds wins -- with one difference: the
first positional argument of every schema here is `self`, and the caller
is the bound method, so the resolver binds the receiver into it.
Why methods need their own table at all. `torch.mul(a, b)` and `a.mul(b)`
reach the same kernels, but they are *different bindings* upstream:
`THPVariable_mul` (a method on TensorBase) and the `_VariableFunctions`
entry are separate C functions with separate signature lists, and
docs/C_SURFACE.md measured the two surfaces separately for that reason --
50 TensorBase members called versus 13 hoisted functions. A method is not
reachable by putting its name in `overloads.json`; nothing looks there.
ORDER IS THE ALGORITHM, as in `overloads.json`. The order here is the
order of the `@overload` declarations for that method in the vendored
tree's own `torch/_C/__init__.pyi` (`class TensorBase`), cross-checked
against what a `TorchDispatchMode` logger on torch 2.13.0 reports for
concrete calls. Places where the two disagree, or where a plausible order
would be the wrong one, are noted per entry below.
Not every TensorBase member is here. Three kinds are elsewhere, for
reasons docs/TENSORBASE.md gives:
* identity (`shape`, `dtype`, `device`, `dim`, `numel`, `size`) is
answered in Rust from the wrapper -- no aten call exists for it;
* `to`/`float`/`long`, `item`, `__bool__`, `__getitem__` and the
autograd-shaped members are Python-level in `bootstrap.py`, because
upstream's binding for them is not a plain overload set either;
* everything not measured as used stays a raising stub.
Provenance: every string is `str(torch.ops.aten.<op>.<ov>._schema)` from
torch 2.13.0, transcribed. `pytests/verify_schemas.py` re-derives both
tables from an installed upstream torch and diffs, so a transcription
slip or an upstream drift fails loudly instead of silently binding the
wrong overload.
An entry here does not promise a kernel. `le`/`__le__` resolve correctly
and then raise `aten op not implemented in torch._C shim: aten.le.Scalar`
from `aten.rs`, which is the point: a resolved-but-unimplemented overload
is a precise work item, where a missing table entry is only a vague one.
`div.Tensor_mode` has been in that state since this table was written.
`softmax` is the one measured method deliberately left out of *this*
table. `F.softmax` spells itself `input.softmax(dim)`, so it would
belong here -- but the parser-level key is `aten.softmax.int` while the
key upstream's dispatcher actually sees is `aten._softmax.default`
(measured, docs/NN_SURFACE.md §6). Listing `softmax.int` would name a
work item this shim will never implement, which is worse than naming
none. Same reasoning as `to.dtype` versus `_to_copy` in
`_install_tensor_conversions`. `Tensor.softmax` is still installed --
as a Python-level composite, `_install_tensor_softmax` in bootstrap.py,
which calls `_to_copy` then `_softmax.default` exactly as the measured
dispatch trace shows, the same way `to`/`item`/`__getitem__` are.
`split` is the one entry here whose schemas do not share one op name --
`aten::split.Tensor` and `aten::split_with_sizes` are genuinely different
aten ops, not two overloads of the same op. Upstream's own
`torch/_tensor.py:Tensor.split` is exactly this branch (measured with a
`TorchDispatchMode` logger): `isinstance(split_size, int)` picks
`torch._VF.split`, anything else picks `torch._VF.split_with_sizes`. The
resolver here does not care whether a key's schemas share an op name --
it tries each schema in order and keys off whichever one binds -- so
listing both under `split` reproduces that exact branch: an int argument
binds `split.Tensor` (kernel present), a list/tuple binds
`split_with_sizes` (kernel absent, named precisely). `split_with_sizes`
also gets its own entry, because `Tensor.split_with_sizes` is a real
method upstream too. This is unlike `softmax` above -- there the parser
key and the dispatch key genuinely disagree and no table entry could ever
be right; here both keys are real and simply depend on the argument.
The seven entries added for Mixtral (docs/GROUPED_MM.md §6.4), and what
is worth knowing about each:
* `__idiv__` is not a typo for `__itruediv__`. `torch/_tensor.py:1115`
assigns `Tensor.__itruediv__ = _C.TensorBase.__idiv__` -- the C name
kept the Python 2 spelling. Measured: `x /= t` dispatches
`aten.div_.Tensor`. MoE normalises router weights with `/=`.
* `div_` carries the `_mode` overloads for the same reason `div` does:
`str? rounding_mode` has no default, so those two only bind when the
caller passes `rounding_mode=`. Neither `_mode` overload has a kernel
here, so they name a work item rather than compute one.
* `div_.Scalar` is listed and upstream never reaches it: measured,
`x.div_(2.0)` dispatches `aten.div_.Tensor`, because torch's frontend
wraps the number into a tensor before it picks an overload and this
resolver does not. Exactly the divergence `div`/`add`/`sub` already
have, and the one docs/GROUPED_MM.md §6.2 records for
`floor_divide.Scalar`.
* `ge`/`__ge__` complete the comparison set -- `le`, `lt`, `gt`, `eq`
and `ne` all had both spellings and `ge` had neither. Both of `ge`'s
overloads now have a kernel: `ge.Tensor` was the one missing member
of the comparison family (`le.Tensor`, `lt.Tensor` and `gt.Tensor`
all had one), so `x >= tensor` resolved here and then refused inside
`_aten_dispatch`. Closed in docs/VIEWS.md §1.
* `clamp_` follows the `.pyi` order -- Tensor overload first -- and the
measurement agrees with it rather than contradicting it:
`x.clamp_(max=6)` lands on `aten.clamp_.default` because an `int`
does not bind `Tensor? max`, and `x.clamp_(max=tensor)` lands on
`aten.clamp_.Tensor`. Same shape as `masked_fill`, whose Tensor-first
order has held since this table was written. `clamp_.Tensor` has no
kernel here.
* `masked_fill_` is `masked_fill`'s in-place twin, same order, and its
`.Tensor` overload is likewise kernel-less.
* `add_`/`sub_`/`mul_`/`neg_`/`exp_`/`relu_` and the three `__i*__`
dunders arrived together (docs/ARCH20.md §8), and the gap they
closed is worth naming: `aten.add_.Tensor` had had a kernel since
docs/TAIL.md and `aten.relu_.default` since docs/KERNELS.md, and
neither name was reachable from Python -- `x += y` raised
`NotImplementedError: TensorBase.__iadd__`, on a kernel that was
there and golden-compared. These are the most common mutations in
the language and every one of them refused.
* The `__i*__` dunders list the same schemas as their named siblings
because upstream's `.pyi` gives them the same one signature
(`__iadd__(self, other: Tensor | Number | _complex)`). `x += y` and
`x.add_(y)` are the same call, and `torch/_tensor.py` does not even
define `__iadd__` -- it inherits `_C.TensorBase.__iadd__`, which is
why a missing entry here made the operator raise rather than fall
back to `__add__`.
* `Scalar` overloads are listed for all three arithmetic families and
upstream's *dispatcher* never names them: measured, `t.add_(2)`
reports `aten.add_.Tensor`, because `add_.Scalar`'s
CompositeExplicitAutograd body wraps the number and redispatches.
The same divergence `div_.Scalar` records just above, and it is the
parser this table reproduces, not the dispatcher. They have kernels
here so that `x += 2` computes rather than refusing.
* `clamp` joins `clamp_`, in the same Tensor-first `.pyi` order, and
only its `default` overload has a kernel -- `clamp.Tensor` names a
work item. `mamba` asked for the out-of-place spelling; the in-place
one had been implemented since docs/OPS8.md.
`chunk` and `__setitem__` were part of the same Mixtral batch and are
*not* here: both are Python-level members in bootstrap.py, for the
reasons given there. `chunk` is `CompositeImplicitAutograd` upstream and
lowers to `split.Tensor` or `split_with_sizes` depending on its
arguments, so no single key is right; `__setitem__` is a walk over the
index like `__getitem__`, not one call.
docs/TRIL.md added `amax`, `tril` and `triu` here, mirroring
`overloads.json` schema-for-schema (its README carries the accounting).
`Tensor.amax` is the case worth remembering: the kernel behind it landed
a round earlier and was golden-compared from the day it landed, while
*both* Python spellings raised. The harness dispatches by key and cannot
see a missing name; what caught it was a smoke test written by the round
that created the gap, asserting the refusal by name so that adding the
entry would break it. It did, and updating it was the notification.
The `min` entry's `.dim` and `.other` schemas are no longer kernel-less
-- docs/SPELLINGS.md §7.2 listed them here precisely so they would refuse
by name, and docs/TRIL.md §3 implemented both. `torch.min(x, dim=0)` and
`torch.min(x, y)` compute now.
